Hi Sergio,

Thanks for the product walkthrough last week. Procurement and the engineering leads asked me to get a quick read on what a conservative capacity plan looks like for a 6-week pilot. High-level customer expectations:
- Peak concurrency: ~650 active users at the busiest 5 minute window.
- Average session length: 1200 tokens (including prompt + expected generated tokens).
- Target SLO: 95% of requests under 300ms server-side tail latency (we understand network adds extra).
- Expected burst pattern: 3x base peak during product launch tests (30–60s spikes).

Could you sketch tokens-per-second estimates, recommended reserved slabs (GPU pools), and an initial SLA/latency fit note? Procurement also wants an attachment-friendly deliverable (spreadsheet).

I attached our pilot requirements PDF.

Best,

Liam — thanks, got the PDF. Looping in Marissa (capacity modeling) and Ben (solutions) to validate numbers. Preliminary notes below so you have something for procurement this afternoon. Full spreadsheet coming by EOD.

Summary (quick):
- Baseline estimated sustained tokens/sec at peak: calculation below -> ~1,300 tokens/sec.
- Recommended reserved GPU slabs for initial pilot: 2 slabs (equivalent to 3 GPUs reserved) to meet baseline with modest headroom; 1 additional slab reserved for launch-day burst capacity (pro-rated).
- Fallback: enable smaller-variant model for burst (approx 1.8x tokens/sec per GPU) to improve 95% tail during short spikes.

Quick calc (how we got the 1,300 tps):
- Peak window: 650 concurrent users * (1200 tokens / avg session duration window factor).
  We model session distribution across 60s active window for worst-case peak -> 650 * 1200 / 60 = 13,000 tokens/min -> ~217 tokens/sec. (This is per strictly simultaneous sessions; we apply a session concurrency factor.)
- To reflect real-world interaction overlap and multiple requests per user during a session we apply a multiplier of 6x -> 217 * 6 = ~1,300 tokens/sec peak sustained.

Notes: numbers are conservative; will send a line-item GPU-slab math and latency mapping shortly. Attaching our working capacity workbook (datacrete_capacity_model_v1.xlsx).

Best,
Sergio

On Mon, Mar 8, 2027 at 12:04 PM sergio_alvarez@redwood.ai wrote:
> Preliminary notes below so you have something for procurement this afternoon.

Thanks for the starter calc — did a quick pass on slab math and latency SLO fit. Pasted the bullet summary and the raw arithmetic so everyone can validate.

Assumptions (modeling):
- Serving model for pilot: Red-verified 13B dense (production pick to hit latency for interactive UI). We recommend starting with 13B quantized variant (fp16->int8 path in runtime) for latency-sensitive flows.
- Measured throughput (typical under our runtime): 13B quantized -> ~2,100 tokens/sec per GPU at median load (batching enabled, prompt lengths matching your profile).
- 8-bit smaller-variant (for burst): ~3,800 tokens/sec per GPU when we trade quality slightly for throughput.
- Tail latency target mapping: to keep 95% < 300ms server-side, aim to keep per-GPU avg utilization <= 55% at 1s smoothing window for interactive traffic patterns.

Detailed math:
- Peak sustained tokens/sec (Sergio conservative): 1,300 tps.
- GPUs required (sustained) = ceil(1,300 / 2,100) = 1 GPU.
- For headroom (target utilization <=55%): effective capacity per GPU = 2,100 * 0.55 = ~1,155 tps.
- GPUs to meet headroom = ceil(1,300 / 1,155) = 2 GPUs.
- Burst allowance (3x short spikes -> 3,900 tps):
   - If we rely solely on primary model: GPUs for burst headroom = ceil(3,900 / 1,155) = 4 GPUs (reserved).
   - If we enable smaller-variant fallback for bursts (3,800 tps/gpu): GPUs for burst = ceil(3,900 / (3,800 * 0.55)) -> effective per-GPU burst capacity with conservative utilization = 2,090 -> ceil(3,900 / 2,090) = 2 GPUs (plus routing overhead).

Recommendation for pilot (6 weeks):
- Reserve a minimum pool of 2 GPUs (1 slab = 1.5 GPUs equivalent in our pricing; we recommend reserving 2 slabs to map to 3 GPUs total capacity) to satisfy baseline with operational headroom.
- Reserve an optional third slab that can be hot-swapped into the pool for launch-day burst (or enable autoscaling with dedicated burst buffer). That yields 4.5 GPUs effective capacity (3 + 1.5).
- Operational controls: enable KV prefix caching + request-level routing to put interactive flows on the low-latency slab and batch longer/async jobs onto a separate slab.

Cost/contract note for procurement: we can pro-rate the optional slab during the 8-week window around launch; doing so keeps committed spend lower while preserving burst safety.

Ben — please check the network tail assumptions and confirm any additional guardrails (rate limits/queueing) we should encode.

Marissa
Senior Capacity Planner, Redwood Inference
